summary: Eigenvalue problem. Use the slider on the graph to step through the eigenfunctions.

methods.name: Three cases for λ
methods.reason: The general solution of \(y'' + \lambda y = 0\) changes form with the sign of \(\lambda\).

steps.title: Set up the problem
steps.text: Find the values of \(\lambda\) for which the problem has a solution other than \(y = 0\). The form of the solution depends on the sign of \(\lambda\), so treat three cases.

steps.title: Case λ < 0
steps.text: Write \(\lambda = -\mu^2\) with \(\mu > 0\). The solutions are hyperbolic functions. The condition at 0 removes one of them, and the one that is left is never zero (nor is its slope) at \(x = L\), so both constants must vanish: there are no negative eigenvalues.
latex: y = C_1\cosh\mu x + C_2\sinh\mu x \ \Rightarrow\ C_1 = C_2 = 0

steps.title: Case λ = 0
steps.text: The equation is \(y'' = 0\), a straight line. The two conditions force it to be the zero function, so \(\lambda = 0\) is not an eigenvalue.
latex: y = C_1 + C_2 x \ \Rightarrow\ C_1 = C_2 = 0

steps.title: Case λ > 0
steps.text: Write \(\lambda = \mu^2\) with \(\mu > 0\). The condition at 0 gives \(C_1 = 0\). For a non-zero solution the condition at \(L\) then needs \(\sin\mu L = 0\), which happens only for special values of \(\mu\).
latex: y = C_1\cos\mu x + C_2\sin\mu x \ \Rightarrow\ y = C_2\sin\mu x

steps.title: Eigenvalues and eigenfunctions
steps.text: Each allowed \(\mu\) gives one eigenvalue \(\lambda = \mu^2\) and one eigenfunction (any constant multiple also works).

steps.title: Orthogonality
steps.text: Eigenfunctions belonging to different eigenvalues are orthogonal on \([0, L]\). This is what lets a function be expanded in them, exactly as in a Fourier series.

steps.title: Check
steps.text: The first five were substituted into the equation and both boundary conditions.

methods.verify_note: The first five were substituted into the equation and both boundary conditions.
